# Schema

Tables first, then materialized views, then views.

## `categories`

Product categories, one level deep, grouped into departments. Demand seasonality and day-of-week patterns are properties of the category.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `category_id` | smallint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `name` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `department` | text NOT NULL |  |  |

## `inventory`

Current stock per store per product, with that store's restock policy. on_hand is a materialisation of the movement history: it equals the sum of inventory_movements.quantity minus the sum of sale_lines.quantity for the same store and product. That invariant is asserted by a test.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | PK, FK → stores |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK, FK → products |  |
| `on_hand` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |
| `reorder_point` | integer NOT NULL |  | Restock when on_hand falls to or below this. Set per store, because a busy store needs a higher floor than a quiet one. "What should we reorder" means on_hand <= reorder_point unless the question names an explicit number. |
| `reorder_qty` | integer NOT NULL |  | How many units to order when restocking, before rounding up to the supplier's case pack and minimum order quantity. |
| `last_counted_on` | date NOT NULL |  |  |

## `inventory_movements`

Stock movements that are NOT sales: deliveries in, shrinkage out, stock-count corrections. Sales are already recorded in sale_lines and are deliberately not duplicated here — doing so would triple the largest table in the database for no new information. To reconstruct stock history you need both this table and sale_lines.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `movement_id` | bigint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → stores |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | FK → products |  |
| `business_date` | date NOT NULL |  |  |
| `movement_type` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `quantity` | integer NOT NULL |  | Signed. Positive increases stock (a delivery), negative decreases it (shrinkage, a return to the supplier). |
| `reference_type` | text |  |  |
| `reference_id` | bigint |  | Loose reference to the row named by reference_type — a po_id when reference_type is 'purchase_order'. Not a foreign key, because the referent varies. |
| `note` | text |  |  |

## `products`

The product catalogue. Chain-wide: a product is the same product in every store. Per-store stock is in inventory; per-supplier cost is in supplier_prices.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `sku` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `name` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `category_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → categories |  |
| `unit_of_measure` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `pack_size` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |
| `list_price` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | Shelf price (MRP) before any promotion, net of tax, in the currency on supplier_prices.currency. The price actually charged is on sale_lines.unit_price, which may be lower during a promotion. |
| `is_active` | boolean NOT NULL |  |  |
| `discontinued_on` | date |  |  |

## `promotion_products`

Which products a promotion applies to.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `promotion_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK, FK → promotions |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK, FK → products |  |

## `promotions`

Promotional events. Promotions are a real table rather than an invisible multiplier in the seed generator, so unexplained demand spikes are always explainable by a query. Date range is inclusive on both ends.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `promotion_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → stores |  |
| `name` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `discount_pct` | numeric(5,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `starts_on` | date NOT NULL |  |  |
| `ends_on` | date NOT NULL |  |  |

## `purchase_order_lines`

Line items on a purchase order. quantity_received may be less than quantity_ordered on a short delivery.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `po_line_id` | bigint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `po_id` | bigint NOT NULL | FK → purchase_orders |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | FK → products |  |
| `quantity_ordered` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |
| `quantity_received` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |
| `unit_cost` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `line_total` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |

## `purchase_orders`

Orders placed with suppliers. Seeded history exists so that supplier delivery performance is observable — comparing ordered_on to received_on against the contracted supplier_terms.lead_time_days is a real question with a real answer. From Phase 4 the procurement agent writes rows here with source = 'agent', but only after a human approves.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `po_id` | bigint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → stores |  |
| `supplier_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → suppliers |  |
| `status` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `source` | text NOT NULL |  | Who created this order: 'seed' is generated history, 'agent' was drafted by the procurement agent and approved by a human, 'manual' was entered by hand. |
| `ordered_on` | date NOT NULL |  |  |
| `expected_on` | date NOT NULL |  | Delivery date promised at the time of ordering, from the supplier's contracted lead time. received_on is when it actually arrived. |
| `received_on` | date |  |  |
| `subtotal` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `created_by_user_id` | integer | FK → users |  |

## `sale_lines`

Line items. store_id and business_date are copied down from the sales header so that sales-velocity queries never need to join it; the three-column foreign key makes it impossible for those copies to disagree with the header.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sale_line_id` | bigint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `sale_id` | bigint NOT NULL | FK → sales |  |
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → sales |  |
| `business_date` | date NOT NULL | FK → sales |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | FK → products |  |
| `promotion_id` | integer | FK → promotions |  |
| `quantity` | integer NOT NULL |  | Signed: positive on a sale, NEGATIVE on a return. So SUM(quantity) is NET units, not gross units sold. If you want gross, filter to quantity > 0 — or use daily_product_sales, which names units_sold, return_units and net_units separately. |
| `unit_price` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | Price actually charged per unit, after any promotional discount. Compare against products.list_price to see the discount. |
| `unit_cost` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | What this unit cost the business, frozen at the time of sale. Margin is line_total minus quantity * unit_cost. Do not join to supplier_prices for historical margin — that gives today's cost, not the cost then. |
| `discount_amount` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `line_total` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |

## `sale_operators`

Which member of staff rang up which sale. Separated from the sales table and NOT granted to pos_readonly, so the natural-language query interface is structurally incapable of returning who did what. ADR-0002 requires that the agent reports patterns, never people; keeping this out of reach makes that a property of the schema rather than a rule a prompt is trusted to follow. Pattern-level analysis runs as pos_app.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sale_id` | bigint NOT NULL | PK, FK → sales |  |
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → sales |  |
| `business_date` | date NOT NULL | FK → sales |  |
| `user_id` | integer NOT NULL | FK → users |  |

## `sales`

Transaction headers — one row per basket. A refund is a separate row with sale_type = 'return' and negative quantities on its lines. Who rang the sale up is deliberately NOT in this table; see sale_operators.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sale_id` | bigint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → stores |  |
| `sold_at` | timestamp with time zone NOT NULL |  | Exact transaction time, with timezone. Use this only when the time of day matters. For anything aggregated by day, use business_date. |
| `business_date` | date NOT NULL |  | The store's trading day in its own timezone. This is the correct column for every daily, weekly, monthly or year-on-year aggregation. It is not always equal to the UTC date of sold_at. |
| `sale_type` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `tender_type` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `subtotal` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | Sum of the line totals, NET of tax. Equals sum(sale_lines.line_total) for this sale. |
| `discount_total` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | Total promotional discount given on this sale, as a positive number. It has already been taken off subtotal — do not subtract it again. |
| `tax_total` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | GST charged, summed per line at the rate for that product's category. Rates vary by category: staples and fresh produce are 0% or 5%, packaged foods 12%, most household and personal care 18%, aerated drinks 28%. So the effective rate on a basket is a blend and cannot be assumed. |
| `total` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  | What the customer paid: subtotal + tax_total. Revenue questions normally mean subtotal (net of tax); cash-collected questions mean total. |

## `stockout_days`

Days a product was out of stock at a store while customers were still asking for it. This exists to prevent a specific analytical trap: sales are capped by available stock, so the products that stock out — exactly the products a restock question is about — have UNDERSTATED sales velocity. Velocity should be measured over days the product was actually available, which is what v_product_velocity_30d does.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | PK, FK → stores |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK, FK → products |  |
| `business_date` | date NOT NULL | PK |  |

## `stores`

Physical retail locations. The multi-store user interface is deferred (docs/PLAN.md cut list) but store_id is present on every store-scoped table from the start.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store_id` | smallint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `code` | text NOT NULL |  | Short human-readable store code, e.g. ST-01. |
| `name` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `city` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `timezone` | text NOT NULL |  | IANA timezone name. Determines the trading day (business_date) for sales rung up at this store. |
| `opened_on` | date NOT NULL |  |  |

## `supplier_prices`

What a supplier charges for a product, over time. One row per price period. A purchase order proposal records the supplier_price_id it was drafted against, so it can refuse to execute if a newer price now applies.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `supplier_price_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `supplier_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → suppliers |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | FK → products |  |
| `unit_cost` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `currency` | character(3) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `effective_from` | date NOT NULL |  |  |
| `effective_to` | date |  |  |
| `valid_period` | daterange |  | Generated half-open range [effective_from, effective_to). Prefer valid_period @> DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD' over comparing the two date columns by hand — it cannot get the boundary wrong. NULL effective_to is unbounded, so the current price matches any future date. |
| `source` | text NOT NULL |  | Where this row came from. 'seed' is generated data; 'document' is extracted from a real source document in Phase 2. |
| `supersedes_id` | integer | FK → supplier_prices |  |

## `supplier_products`

Which suppliers can supply which products, and the non-temporal facts about that relationship. Price is time-scoped and lives in supplier_prices.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `supplier_product_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `supplier_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → suppliers |  |
| `product_id` | integer NOT NULL | FK → products |  |
| `supplier_sku` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `is_preferred` | boolean NOT NULL |  | Exactly one supplier per product is preferred. Restock proposals default to the preferred supplier. |
| `min_order_qty` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |
| `case_pack` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |

## `supplier_terms`

Commercial terms agreed with a supplier, over time. One row per term period; a renegotiation closes the old row and opens a new one. The exclusion constraint makes overlapping terms impossible, so "what are the terms on date D" always has at most one answer. Gaps ARE allowed: a date with no row means no terms were in force, which is different from the supplier not existing. Phase 2 populates history and provenance from real documents; it does not reshape this table.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `supplier_terms_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `supplier_id` | smallint NOT NULL | FK → suppliers |  |
| `payment_terms_days` | integer NOT NULL |  | Days to pay. 30 means Net 30. |
| `lead_time_days` | integer NOT NULL |  | Contracted days between placing an order and delivery. Actual delivery performance is observable from purchase_orders.ordered_on vs received_on and is not always the same thing. |
| `min_order_value` | numeric(12,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `volume_discount_pct` | numeric(5,2) NOT NULL |  |  |
| `returns_window_days` | integer NOT NULL |  |  |
| `effective_from` | date NOT NULL |  |  |
| `effective_to` | date |  |  |
| `valid_period` | daterange |  |  |
| `source` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `source_note` | text |  |  |
| `supersedes_id` | integer | FK → supplier_terms | The term period this one replaced. Mirrors the supersedes column in corpus/MANIFEST.csv so the database and the document corpus encode version chains the same way. |

## `suppliers`

Suppliers the business buys from. Chain-level, not store-scoped. Commercial terms and prices are NOT here — they are time-scoped and live in supplier_terms and supplier_prices.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `supplier_id` | smallint NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `code` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `name` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `contact_email` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `is_active` | boolean NOT NULL |  |  |

## `users`

Staff accounts and their roles. NOT readable by pos_readonly. Display names are role-and-ordinal labels ("Clerk 03"), never realistic person names — ADR-0002 forbids demoing with employee names, including synthetic ones, in a public repository.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `user_id` | integer NOT NULL | PK |  |
| `username` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `display_name` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `role` | text NOT NULL |  |  |
| `store_id` | smallint | FK → stores | The store this user works at. NULL means chain-wide access. This is the entire data model for role-scoping: scoping is applied when the query is built, never by dropping rows from results afterwards (CLAUDE.md rule 5). |
| `is_active` | boolean NOT NULL |  |  |

## `daily_product_sales` — materialized view

Per store, per product, per trading day sales rollup, derived from sale_lines. Refreshed by `make seed`. Gross, returns and net are named separately so no query has to remember that sale_lines.quantity is signed. Days with no sales have no row.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store_id` | smallint |  |  |
| `product_id` | integer |  |  |
| `business_date` | date |  |  |
| `units_sold` | bigint |  |  |
| `return_units` | bigint |  |  |
| `net_units` | bigint |  |  |
| `gross_revenue` | numeric |  |  |
| `cogs` | numeric |  |  |

## `v_product_velocity_30d` — view

How fast each product sells at each store, over the 30 trading days ending on the most recent day present in the data. units_per_day divides by the days the product was actually AVAILABLE, not by 30, so a product that stocked out is not penalised for the days it could not be sold. One row per row of inventory, including products that sold nothing.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store_id` | smallint |  |  |
| `product_id` | integer |  |  |
| `as_of_date` | date |  |  |
| `units_sold_30d` | numeric |  |  |
| `net_units_30d` | numeric |  |  |
| `revenue_30d` | numeric(12,2) |  |  |
| `stockout_days_30d` | bigint |  |  |
| `available_days_30d` | bigint |  |  |
| `units_per_day` | numeric |  |  |

## `v_stock_status` — view

One row per store per product: what is on the shelf, how fast it moves, how long the shelf will last, who supplies it and on what terms, and how much is already on order. days_of_cover is on_hand divided by daily velocity — low days_of_cover means running out soon. NULL days_of_cover means the product has not sold in the last 30 days, which is different from running out fast.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store_id` | smallint |  |  |
| `product_id` | integer |  |  |
| `sku` | text |  |  |
| `product_name` | text |  |  |
| `category_name` | text |  |  |
| `department` | text |  |  |
| `on_hand` | integer |  |  |
| `reorder_point` | integer |  |  |
| `reorder_qty` | integer |  |  |
| `below_reorder_point` | boolean |  |  |
| `units_per_day` | numeric |  |  |
| `net_units_30d` | numeric |  |  |
| `stockout_days_30d` | bigint |  |  |
| `days_of_cover` | numeric |  |  |
| `preferred_supplier_id` | smallint |  |  |
| `preferred_supplier_name` | text |  |  |
| `lead_time_days` | integer |  |  |
| `payment_terms_days` | integer |  |  |
| `current_unit_cost` | numeric(12,2) |  |  |
| `case_pack` | integer |  |  |
| `min_order_qty` | integer |  |  |
| `on_order_qty` | bigint |  |  |

## `v_supplier_terms_current` — view

The supplier terms in force now — the rows with no end date. For terms as they stood on some past date, query supplier_terms with valid_period @> DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD' instead. A supplier missing from this view has no terms currently in force, which is not the same as having no terms on record.

| Column | Type | Key | Notes |
